Below is the empirical plan I would implement given the question, data, and institutions.

1. Identification Strategy
- Primary strategy for pollution outcomes: Staggered difference-in-differences with an event-study estimator robust to heterogeneous treatment timing (Sun-Abraham interaction-weighted or Callaway–Sant’Anna). This fits the staggered rollout of Supreme Court Action Plans (SCAP), catalytic converter mandates, and National River Conservation Plan (NRCP) across cities/river stretches and years, and allows visualization/tests of pre-trends.
- Strategy for infant health:
  - Reduced-form DiD/event study: effect of air policy adoption on infant mortality.
  - Causal effect of air quality on infant mortality via 2SLS: instrument ambient air pollution (PM, SO2, NO2) with the timing of air policy adoption(s). The first stage is well-motivated mechanically (policies directly target emissions), and the second stage identifies the effect of regulation-induced changes in air quality on infant mortality. I will prefer the catalytic converter mandates as the main instrument (cleaner exclusion), and use SCAP as a complementary instrument with tighter controls and robustness checks.

2. Treatment and Control
- Units and outcomes:
  - Air pollution: city-year panel; outcome is (i) city-year mean of pollutant (PM, SO2, NO2), ideally in logs, from all monitors in the city.
  - Water pollution: monitor-year along rivers; outcomes are BOD (↑ worse), DO (↓ worse), fecal coliforms (↑ worse). For city-year analyses, aggregate river-monitor outcomes to the city-year if needed.
  - Infant health: city-year infant mortality rate (IMR) per 1,000 live births.

- Treatments:
  - Air policy 1: Supreme Court Action Plans (SCAP). Treated if city i has an SCAP active in year t; treatment timing = first year of SCAP enforcement/order for city i.
  - Air policy 2: Catalytic converters (CAT). Treated if city i is in the set mandated to require catalytic converters on new petrol vehicles; timing = 1995 for the 4 metros and 1998 for the 45 additional cities. Define separate indicators for “post CAT” by city.
  - Water policy: National River Conservation Plan (NRCP). Treated if city i on river r has an NRCP-financed project active/commissioned in year t; timing = first operational year of sewage treatment/interception works for that city–river stretch.

- Controls (counterfactuals):
  - For DiD/event studies: not-yet-treated and never-treated cities/monitors in the same years serve as controls. Estimation uses city and year fixed effects, optionally state-by-year FE or state-specific trends, so comparisons are within-city over time relative to concurrent changes in other cities.
  - For water, because of flow spillovers, we include upstream treatment controls and, in robustness, focus on within-river comparisons of treated vs not-yet-treated city–stretches.

- IV (for IMR):
  - Endogenous regressor: city-year ambient air pollution (e.g., ln PM).
  - Instruments: indicators for post-SCAP and post-CAT (separately or jointly), optionally interacted with time-since-treatment to allow flexible first stages.
  - Exclusion priority: use CAT as the primary instrument (narrow channel to emissions from petrol vehicles; fewer direct economic channels). Include SCAP in an overidentified specification with overid tests and robustness.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Parallel trends (DiD): In the absence of a given policy, treated cities (or treated river stretches) would have followed similar pollution and IMR trends as not-yet-treated controls. Plausibility:
  - Policies targeted highly polluted cities, which raises concern about differential pre-trends. The event-study framework directly tests for pre-trend equivalence; we will include state-by-year FE and state-specific linear trends or city-specific linear trends to improve plausibility.
  - For water, river-by-year shocks may differ; we will add river-basin-by-year FE and monitor FE, and control for upstream treatment.

- No anticipatory behavior: Pollution and IMR do not change in advance of the policy because of anticipatory actions. For CAT, this is plausible (mandates apply to new vehicles; pre-buying is limited for existing fleets). For SCAP, some anticipatory compliance is possible; we will test for pre-treatment effects in the leads of the event study.

- Exclusion restriction (IV): Air policies affect infant mortality only through ambient air quality, after conditioning on FE and controls.
  - Strongest for CAT (direct mechanism is tailpipe emissions on new petrol vehicles).
  - Weaker for SCAP (may include industrial closures, fuel switching, transit policies). We will (i) include controls for concurrent policies (water NRCP), (ii) allow flexible city and state trends, (iii) show that SCAP has no effect on placebo outcomes and non-respiratory pollutants unlikely to affect IMR contemporaneously, and (iv) emphasize CAT-based estimates as primary IV.

- SUTVA/no spillovers:
  - Air: cross-city pollutant transport exists but is limited at the city scale relative to within-city sources. We include state-year FE and spatial robustness (dropping neighbors of early-treated metros) to mitigate concern.
  - Water: we explicitly account for upstream treatment and, in robustness, focus on river segments with minimal confounding from upstream dischargers.

- Stable measurement: Changes in monitor networks should not drive results. We add monitor FE in monitor-level regressions and run robustness on balanced panels.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Endogenous policy timing and differential pre-trends:
  - Mitigation: Sun–Abraham event studies with visual and statistical pre-trend tests; include state-by-year FE and state-specific linear trends; control for baseline pollution interacted with year to allow high-pollution places to have different slopes; robustness with Callaway–Sant’Anna ATT(g,t); city-specific linear trends in select specifications.

- Concurrent shocks and policies:
  - Mitigation: Include both air (SCAP, CAT) and water (NRCP) indicators jointly; add year × state FE; control for newspaper pollution attention (Times of India mentions) and corruption proxies; demonstrate no effects on non-targeted pollutants (placebos); show water NRCP has no effect on air pollutants and vice versa.

- Spillovers and measurement/composition:
  - Air: drop border cities near early-treated metros in robustness; cluster standard errors at city level and use spatially robust SE as a check.
  - Water: include upstream-treatment exposure; restrict to monitors with stable locations and to stretches with no upstream project start within ±2 years in robustness; cluster at river-basin.

- Exclusion for IV (policy affects IMR via income/employment):
  - Prefer CAT-only IV; include city-specific linear trends; control for district demographics (interpolated census) and consumption expenditures; demonstrate no impact of air policies on water pollutants and vice versa; placebo on outcomes less sensitive to air (e.g., accidents, if available).

5. R Code Outline
Note: Filenames are placeholders. This outline uses fixest for FE/event studies (sunab) and for IV. It assumes some minimal harmonization keys (city_id, river_id, monitor_id).

```r
# Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # feols + sunab + IV
library(ggplot2)
library(sandwich)

# 1) Load data
air_raw   <- fread("air_monitors_1986_2007.csv")         # monitor_id, city_id, year, pm, so2, no2
water_raw <- fread("water_monitors_1986_2007.csv")       # monitor_id, city_id, river_id, year, bod, do, fecal
policy    <- fread("policy_city_year.csv")               # city_id, year, scap_active, cat_active, nrcp_active, scap_start, cat_start, nrcp_start
imr       <- fread("infant_mortality_city_year.csv")     # city_id, year, imr
demo      <- fread("district_census_controls.csv")       # district_id, year, literacy, female_edu, pop, consumption
city_x    <- fread("city_district_state_crosswalk.csv")  # city_id, district_id, state_id

# 2) Construct city-year pollution aggregates
# Air: average across monitors within city-year (monitor FE used in robustness)
air <- air_raw[ , .(
  pm  = mean(pm,  na.rm=TRUE),
  so2 = mean(so2, na.rm=TRUE),
  no2 = mean(no2, na.rm=TRUE),
  n_mon_air = .N
), by = .(city_id, year)]

# Water: city-year means (alternative: monitor-level regressions)
water <- water_raw[ , .(
  bod   = mean(bod,  na.rm=TRUE),
  do    = mean(do,   na.rm=TRUE),
  fecal = mean(fecal,na.rm=TRUE),
  n_mon_water = .N
), by = .(city_id, year)]

# 3) Merge to analysis panel
panel <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by=c("city_id","year"), all=TRUE),
                list(air, water, policy, imr))
panel <- merge(panel, city_x, by="city_id", all.x=TRUE)
panel <- merge(panel, demo, by=c("district_id","year"), all.x=TRUE)

# 4) Variable construction
panel[, ln_pm   := log(pm)]
panel[, ln_so2  := log(so2)]
panel[, ln_no2  := log(no2)]
panel[, ln_bod  := log(bod)]
panel[, ln_fecal:= log(fecal)]
panel[, t       := year - min(year, na.rm=TRUE)]

# Treatment timing for Sun–Abraham: first-year-of-treatment by policy (group)
# If never treated, leave NA (sunab handles)
panel[, scap_start_city := ifelse(scap_active==1 & (is.na(shift(scap_active,1,type="lag")) | shift(scap_active,1,type="lag")==0),
                                  year, NA), by=city_id]
scap_start <- panel[!is.na(scap_start_city), .(scap_start=min(scap_start_city)), by=city_id]
panel <- merge(panel, scap_start, by="city_id", all.x=TRUE)

panel[, cat_start_city := ifelse(cat_active==1 & (is.na(shift(cat_active,1,type="lag")) | shift(cat_active,1,type="lag")==0),
                                 year, NA), by=city_id]
cat_start <- panel[!is.na(cat_start_city), .(cat_start=min(cat_start_city)), by=city_id]
panel <- merge(panel, cat_start, by="city_id", all.x=TRUE)

panel[, nrcp_start_city := ifelse(nrcp_active==1 & (is.na(shift(nrcp_active,1,type="lag")) | shift(nrcp_active,1,type="lag")==0),
                                  year, NA), by=city_id]
nrcp_start <- panel[!is.na(nrcp_start_city), .(nrcp_start=min(nrcp_start_city)), by=city_id]
panel <- merge(panel, nrcp_start, by="city_id", all.x=TRUE)

# State-year FE helper
panel[, state_year := interaction(state_id, year, drop=TRUE)]

# 5) Main event-study: effect of SCAP on ln(PM)
# Sun-Abraham using sunab(group=first_treat_year, time=year)
es_scap_pm <- feols(
  ln_pm ~ sunab(scap_start, year) + cat_active + nrcp_active +
    literacy + female_edu + consumption |
    city_id + year + state_id[t],
  data = panel,
  cluster = ~ city_id
)

# Plot event-study coefficients
iplot(es_scap_pm, ref.line = 0)

# 6) Main event-study: effect of CAT on ln(NO2)
es_cat_no2 <- feols(
  ln_no2 ~ sunab(cat_start, year) + scap_active + nrcp_active +
    literacy + female_edu + consumption |
    city_id + year + state_id[t],
  data = panel,
  cluster = ~ city_id
)

# 7) Water policy effect on ln(BOD) (city-year)
es_nrcp_bod <- feols(
  ln_bod ~ sunab(nrcp_start, year) + scap_active + cat_active +
    literacy + female_edu + consumption |
    city_id + year + state_id[t],
  data = panel,
  cluster = ~ city_id
)

# 8) Reduced-form effect of air policies on IMR
es_imr_scap <- feols(
  imr ~ sunab(scap_start, year) + cat_active + nrcp_active +
    literacy + female_edu + consumption |
    city_id + year + state_id[t],
  data = panel,
  cluster = ~ city_id
)

es_imr_cat <- feols(
  imr ~ sunab(cat_start, year) + scap_active + nrcp_active +
    literacy + female_edu + consumption |
    city_id + year + state_id[t],
  data = panel,
  cluster = ~ city_id
)

# 9) IV: Effect of air quality (ln PM) on IMR, instrumented by air policies
# Preferred: CAT-only IV
iv_imr_pm_cat <- feols(
  imr ~ 1 | ln_pm ~ cat_active + scap_active,   # include both for first-stage strength; report CAT-only as primary in robustness
  data = panel,
  fixef = ~ city_id + year + state_id[t],
  cluster = ~ city_id
)

summary(iv_imr_pm_cat, stage=1)  # check first-stage F-stat
summary(iv_imr_pm_cat)

# 10) Robustness check examples

# (a) Callaway–Sant’Anna ATT for SCAP on ln(PM) using not-yet-treated controls
# Prepare minimal dataset
library(did)
did_dat <- panel[!is.na(ln_pm), .(city_id, year, ln_pm, scap_start)]
did_dat[, G := ifelse(is.na(scap_start), 0, scap_start)]
att <- att_gt(yname="ln_pm", tname="year", idname="city_id",
              gname="G", data=did_dat, panel=TRUE, control_group="notyettreated")
summary(att)
ggdid(aggte(att, type = "dynamic"))

# (b) Placebo: water policy on ln(PM) and air policy on ln(BOD)
placebo_air <- feols(ln_pm ~ sunab(nrcp_start, year) | city_id + year + state_id[t],
                     data=panel, cluster=~city_id)
placebo_water <- feols(ln_bod ~ sunab(scap_start, year) + sunab(cat_start, year) | city_id + year + state_id[t],
                       data=panel, cluster=~city_id)

# (c) Balanced air-monitor panel robustness at monitor level with monitor FE
air_bal <- air_raw[ , .N, by=.(monitor_id)][N == max(N)]$monitor_id
air_m <- merge(air_raw[monitor_id %in% air_bal], policy, by=c("city_id","year"), all.x=TRUE)
air_m[, ln_pm := log(pm)]
es_monitor <- feols(
  ln_pm ~ sunab(scap_start, year) + cat_active + nrcp_active |
    monitor_id + year + state_id[t],
  data = merge(air_m, city_x, by="city_id"),
  cluster = ~ city_id
)
```

6. Expected Results
- Air regulations:
  - SCAP: Moderate to large reductions in PM and SO2/NO2 in treated cities relative to controls; order of magnitude 10–25% decline in PM over 3–5 years post adoption.
  - Catalytic converters: Noticeable declines in NO2 (tailpipe NOx) and smaller declines in PM (petrol vehicles contribute less to PM than diesel/industry); order of 5–15% NO2 reduction in treated cities.
- Water regulation (NRCP): Limited or no average impact on BOD/DO/fecal coliforms at city river monitors, due to fragmented implementation, non-point discharges, operation/maintenance issues, and upstream inflows.
- Infant health:
  - Reduced-form: Air policy adoption lowers IMR modestly in treated cities (couple of IMR points per 1,000 over several years).
  - IV elasticity: A 10 µg/m3 reduction in PM associated with roughly 0.5–1.5 fewer infant deaths per 1,000 live births (about 1–3% of mean IMR in the 1990s), with larger effects in high-baseline-pollution cities.

- Why success differs across domains: Impacts concentrated where enforcement is centralized and judicially backed (SCAP, CAT); weak/fragmented implementation in water policy yields small/no gains. Heterogeneity tests should show larger air-policy impacts in low-corruption states and cities with higher press attention and stronger SPCBs, and muted or null effects for NRCP even in such places.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
- C1: Parallel trends supported by pre-treatment leads (event-study) — 1 if pre-trends are flat, else 0. Tentative: 1 for air, 0/1 for water depending on river controls.
- C2: No anticipation — 1 for CAT (mandate on new vehicles), 0.5 for SCAP (some anticipatory compliance possible).
- C3: No major spillovers/interference — 0.5 for air (some regional transport), 0.5 for water (up/downstream). We model upstream for water and add spatial robustness for air.
- C4: Exclusion restriction for IV — 1 for CAT-based IV; 0.5 for SCAP-based IV (mitigated with controls and robustness).
- C5: Stable measurement/composition — 0.5 given evolving monitor networks; improved to 1 in robustness with monitor FE and balanced samples.

Overall, the combination of (i) staggered DiD/event studies with strong FE structure and (ii) a CAT-based IV for air quality’s effect on IMR provides a credible design. Heterogeneity by enforcement/corruption helps explain divergence between air and water policy performance.
